questions.text: Do you work or are you a student at the moment?

areSample.answer: I'm currently working full-time as a software engineer at a mid-sized product company.
areSample.reason: I went into this field because I genuinely enjoy breaking down complex problems into clean, practical solutions.
areSample.example: Just this week, for instance, I redesigned our onboarding workflow to cut page loading times almost in half.

questions.text: What do you find most rewarding about your work or studies?

areSample.answer: For me, the most gratifying part is seeing something I've built actually make someone's daily routine easier.
areSample.reason: When your work stays abstract, it's easy to lose motivation, whereas direct feedback keeps me energised.
areSample.example: A few months ago, a user messaged our support team saying a small shortcut we added saved her hours every Friday.

questions.text: Do you prefer working alone or as part of a team?

areSample.answer: Honestly, I thrive on a balance of both, though I lean slightly towards solo work during the early stages.
areSample.reason: Quiet stretches allow me to think deeply without interruption, while teamwork helps spot blind spots I'd otherwise miss.
areSample.example: Usually I'll draft a technical plan on my own in the morning and then bounce it off two colleagues after lunch.

questions.text: What part of your typical workday or study day do you find most challenging?

areSample.answer: Without question, the trickiest part is dealing with constant context switching between meetings and focused tasks.
areSample.reason: Once my concentration is broken, it often takes fifteen or twenty minutes just to rebuild my train of thought.
areSample.example: On Wednesdays we have back-to-back check-ins, so I've started blocking out two hours early in the morning purely for deep work.

questions.text: Would you like to change your career or field of study in the future?
ideaHintsEn: staying in the sector vs pivoting

areSample.answer: I don't see myself leaving the technology sector altogether, but I'd love to shift gradually towards mentoring and education.
areSample.reason: Helping junior colleagues click with a difficult concept gives me a different kind of satisfaction from coding alone.
areSample.example: Last spring I ran a short internal workshop on testing, and I enjoyed preparing for it far more than I expected.

questions.text: Where is your hometown, and what is it like?

areSample.answer: I'm originally from a bustling coastal city in central Vietnam that blends laid-back beach life with fast-growing urban districts.
areSample.reason: Because the sea is only fifteen minutes from the city centre, the whole place feels noticeably airier than larger inland metropolises.
areSample.example: On warm evenings, you'll see families strolling along the promenade while fishermen haul in small boats further down the bay.

questions.text: What do you like most about living there?

areSample.answer: What I appreciate most is the strong sense of neighbourhood warmth combined with easy access to the outdoors.
areSample.reason: People still greet their neighbours by name, which stops the city from feeling anonymous even as it expands.
areSample.example: Whenever I go back, the lady at the corner coffee stall still remembers I take mine iced with very little sugar.

questions.text: Has your hometown changed much since you were a child?

areSample.answer: It's changed almost beyond recognition over the past fifteen years, especially along the riverfront.
areSample.reason: A surge in domestic tourism and private investment has replaced low-rise shophouses with gleaming hotels and wide boulevards.
areSample.example: The empty stretch where my friends and I used to fly kites after school is now lined with cafés and boutique apartments.

questions.text: Is your hometown a good place for young people to live?

areSample.answer: On the whole, yes, particularly for young professionals who can work remotely or who value work-life balance.
areSample.reason: Rent and everyday expenses are far more reasonable than in the capital, though specialised corporate roles can still be scarce.
areSample.example: Several university friends of mine moved back there recently because they could keep their city salaries while living ten minutes from the beach.

questions.text: Do you live in a house or a flat at the moment?

areSample.answer: I live in a compact two-bedroom flat on the ninth floor of a modern residential block.
areSample.reason: Renting a flat suits my schedule far better than a standalone house because building maintenance and security are handled for me.
areSample.example: I also get a decent breeze up there and a clear view over a tree-lined avenue, which keeps traffic noise to a minimum.

questions.text: Which room in your home do you spend the most time in?

areSample.answer: Undoubtedly the open-plan living area, which doubles as my workspace during the week.
areSample.reason: It has floor-to-ceiling windows facing east, so the natural light keeps me alert in the mornings without needing harsh overhead lamps.
areSample.example: Most evenings I just push my laptop aside, brew a pot of herbal tea, and read on the sofa by the balcony door.

questions.text: If you could change one thing about your current home, what would it be?

areSample.answer: I'd definitely expand the kitchen, because the counter space is rather cramped when I try to cook properly.
areSample.reason: I love preparing fresh meals from scratch, yet having barely enough room for a chopping board makes weeknight cooking fiddly.
areSample.example: Last Sunday I made a big batch of noodle soup and ended up lining up half the ingredients on the dining table.

questions.text: What kind of home would you ideally like to live in one day?

areSample.answer: Ideally, I'd love a modest terraced house with a small courtyard garden in a quiet suburb.
areSample.reason: Having a patch of greenery to grow herbs and sit outside would give me a sense of calm that high-rise living rarely offers.
areSample.example: Nothing grand at all—just a bright kitchen opening onto a wooden deck where friends could gather for weekend barbecues.

questions.text: What does a typical weekday morning look like for you?

areSample.answer: I'm quite a creature of habit, so I usually get up around half past six and start with twenty minutes of stretching.
areSample.reason: Easing into the day without checking notifications immediately stops me from feeling rushed before work has even begun.
areSample.example: After that, I make myself a strong black coffee, skim a couple of news headlines, and sit down at my desk by eight.

questions.text: Which part of the day do you feel most productive?

areSample.answer: My energy peaks between nine and noon, which is when my thinking feels sharpest.
areSample.reason: By late afternoon decision fatigue tends to creep in, so tackling demanding tasks early makes a noticeable difference to my output.
areSample.example: Whenever I have to write a detailed report or study dense reading passages, I always guard that morning window fiercely.

questions.text: How different is your weekend routine from your weekday schedule?

areSample.answer: Weekends are far less rigid, although I still avoid sleeping past eight so I don't throw off my body clock.
areSample.reason: Leaving large chunks of Saturday unscheduled helps me recharge mentally after five tightly planned days.
areSample.example: Typically I'll linger over brunch with friends on Saturday morning and keep Sunday afternoon for groceries and a long walk.

questions.text: Would you like to change anything about your current routine?

areSample.answer: I'd really like to wind down earlier in the evenings instead of letting screen time spill past eleven.
areSample.reason: Whenever I stay up watching short clips, I wake up groggy and end up relying on extra caffeine the next morning.
areSample.example: I've recently tried leaving my phone to charge in the living room so I'm nudged to pick up a paperback instead.

questions.text: What piece of technology do you rely on most in your everyday life?

areSample.answer: Aside from my laptop for work, I'd say my smartphone is practically indispensable throughout the day.
areSample.reason: It has quietly absorbed half a dozen separate tools—from banking and maps to boarding passes and language flashcards.
areSample.example: Just yesterday I paid for groceries, checked a train delay, and reviewed thirty vocabulary cards while waiting at the dentist.

questions.text: Do you enjoy keeping up with the latest gadgets and tech releases?

areSample.answer: I enjoy reading about new breakthroughs, though I'm definitely not an early adopter who queues for every launch.
areSample.reason: Most annual upgrades feel fairly incremental, and first-generation devices often come with pricey teething problems.
areSample.example: I kept my previous phone for nearly four years and only replaced it once the battery could barely last till evening.

questions.text: Has technology made your daily life easier or more stressful?

areSample.answer: It's a bit of a double-edged sword: logistically it's far easier, yet mentally it can feel relentless.
areSample.reason: Being reachable at all hours blurs the line between personal downtime and work obligations unless you set firm boundaries.
areSample.example: Switching off work chat notifications after seven in the evening was the single best adjustment I've made all year.

questions.text: How do you usually handle a technical problem when a device stops working?
ideaHintsEn: knowing when to seek a repair shop

areSample.answer: I usually try to troubleshoot it myself first by restarting the device and looking up the exact error message online.
areSample.reason: Nine times out of ten, someone on a community forum has already bumped into the same glitch and shared a straightforward fix.
areSample.example: Last month my laptop Wi-Fi vanished after an update, and a five-minute driver reset from a forum thread saved me a trip to a repair shop.

questions.text: How do you usually travel around your city?

areSample.answer: For most short trips I take a motorbike or ride-hailing service, though I've been using the bus much more lately.
areSample.reason: Driving in heavy rush-hour traffic can be exhausting, whereas sitting on a bus lets me switch off and listen to podcasts.
areSample.example: Whenever I head into the city centre on rainy afternoons, I gladly leave my bike at home and hop on the express route instead.

questions.text: What do you think of the public transport system where you live?

areSample.answer: It's steadily improving and remarkably affordable, though coverage outside the main corridors is still patchy.
areSample.reason: Buses often get caught in the same gridlock as private vehicles, which makes arrival times somewhat unpredictable during peak hours.
areSample.example: That said, the newer electric bus routes with live tracking apps have made commuting across town far more reliable than it used to be.

questions.text: Do you prefer travelling by train or by bus for longer journeys?

areSample.answer: I'd pick the train every single time for journeys lasting more than two or three hours.
areSample.reason: Trains give you space to stretch your legs, a smoother ride for reading, and far less risk of motion sickness than coaches.
areSample.example: I took a coastal train south last autumn, and watching the hills roll past from the dining car felt like part of the holiday itself.

questions.text: What would encourage more people in your area to use public transport?

areSample.answer: Above all, punctual service and better first-and-last-mile connections would make the biggest difference.
areSample.reason: Most commuters don't mind taking a bus or train, but they're put off by walking fifteen minutes in blistering heat to reach a stop.
areSample.example: Adding shaded pavements, dedicated bus lanes, and a single contactless travel card would win over a huge number of daily drivers.

questions.text: Do you make an effort to recycle or reduce waste at home?

areSample.answer: Yes, I try to focus on cutting down waste at the source rather than just sorting rubbish afterwards.
areSample.reason: Recycling systems aren't always thorough locally, so avoiding single-use packaging altogether feels like the more reliable habit.
areSample.example: I keep a foldable tote bag in my backpack and always bring my own stainless-steel cup when I grab takeaway coffee.

questions.text: Did you learn much about environmental protection when you were at school?

areSample.answer: To be honest, it was mostly covered in brief textbook chapters rather than through hands-on projects.
areSample.reason: Back then, exam subjects took priority, so environmental topics rarely went beyond basic slogans about saving water and electricity.
areSample.example: The one memorable exception was a clean-up morning our biology teacher organised along a nearby canal, which really opened my eyes to plastic litter.

questions.text: What is the most noticeable environmental issue in your city?

areSample.answer: Without doubt, air quality and urban heat are the two problems residents feel most acutely.
areSample.reason: Dense vehicle emissions combined with rapid construction leave very little green cover to cool the streets or trap fine dust.
areSample.example: On dry winter mornings, you can actually see a grey haze hanging over the skyline before you even check an air-quality app.

questions.text: Do you think young people today care more about the environment than previous generations?
ideaHintsEn: vocal online vs frugal habits of elders

areSample.answer: Younger people are certainly more vocal about climate issues, though older generations often practised sustainability without calling it that.
areSample.reason: My grandparents' generation repaired clothes, reused jars, and wasted almost no food simply out of thrift rather than activism.
areSample.example: So while my peers swap tips about zero-waste brands online, my grandmother still washes and reuses glass bottles better than any of us.

questions.text: Do you enjoy reading in your free time?

areSample.answer: I really do, especially in the evenings when I want a slower pace after staring at screens all day.
areSample.reason: Reading demands a deeper, calmer kind of attention that leaves my mind refreshed rather than overstimulated.
areSample.example: Right now I'm working my way through a collection of popular-science essays about how cities adapt to extreme weather.

questions.text: Do you prefer printed books or e-books?

areSample.answer: I'm fond of physical books for favourite novels, yet I rely on an e-reader far more in practice.
areSample.reason: When I read in English, being able to tap an unfamiliar phrase for an instant definition keeps me in the flow without reaching for my phone.
areSample.example: It's also a lifesaver on flights, since I can carry half a dozen hefty non-fiction titles in my jacket pocket.

questions.text: What kinds of books did you enjoy reading as a child?

areSample.answer: As a kid, I was completely hooked on illustrated mystery series and children's science encyclopaedias.
areSample.reason: They fed my curiosity about how everyday things worked while still feeling like entertainment rather than homework.
areSample.example: I still remember borrowing the same battered atlas from our local library three times in a row just to memorise capital cities.

questions.text: Where is your favourite place to read?

areSample.answer: Surprisingly, I read best in a calm neighbourhood café with a gentle hum of background chatter.
areSample.reason: Complete silence at home sometimes makes me drowsy, whereas a light buzz around me helps anchor my focus.
areSample.example: There's a small bookshop café near my flat with wooden booths by the window where I often lose track of two hours on a Saturday.

questions.text: Do you enjoy cooking, or do you prefer eating out?

areSample.answer: I genuinely enjoy cooking on weekends, though during hectic weekdays I do lean on local eateries now and then.
areSample.reason: Preparing a meal at home lets me control the freshness and seasoning, and chopping vegetables is surprisingly therapeutic after a long shift.
areSample.example: Most Sundays I roast a tray of seasonal vegetables and simmer a big pot of curry to cover my lunches till Wednesday.

questions.text: What kind of food is your region or country famous for?

areSample.answer: Vietnamese cuisine is best known for its bright balance of sweet, sour, salty, and savoury flavours backed by heaps of fresh herbs.
areSample.reason: Rather than relying on heavy sauces, cooks build depth through slow-simmered broths and crisp raw greens added right before serving.
areSample.example: In my hometown, for example, locals are fiercely proud of a turmeric noodle dish topped with toasted peanuts and crispy rice crackers.

questions.text: Have your eating habits changed much over the past few years?

areSample.answer: They've become noticeably more mindful since my university days, when I basically survived on instant noodles and iced milk tea.
areSample.reason: I started noticing how directly heavy lunches or sugary snacks dragged down my afternoon concentration.
areSample.example: Nowadays I make sure half my plate is vegetables, and I've swapped afternoon pastries for roasted almonds and fruit.

questions.text: Do you like trying unfamiliar dishes from other countries?

areSample.answer: Absolutely—sampling unfamiliar cuisines is honestly one of my favourite ways to learn about another culture.
areSample.reason: Spices and cooking methods tell you so much about a region's climate and history without needing a single guidebook.
areSample.example: Last month a colleague introduced me to Ethiopian injera bread with spiced lentils, and I immediately went home to look up the recipe.

questions.text: What kind of weather do you enjoy most?

areSample.answer: I'm happiest in crisp, dry autumn weather—somewhere around twenty degrees with a gentle breeze and soft sunshine.
areSample.reason: When it's neither sweltering nor freezing, you can spend hours walking outdoors without breaking into a sweat or bundling up in heavy layers.
areSample.example: Whenever we get a rare cool spell in November, I immediately plan a long bike ride along the river.

questions.text: Does the weather usually affect your mood or energy levels?

areSample.answer: More than I'd like to admit, yes—several overcast, humid days in a row definitely make me feel a bit sluggish.
areSample.reason: Bright morning light acts as a natural pick-me-up, whereas grey skies trick my brain into wanting to stay under a blanket.
areSample.example: During the monsoon season, I usually turn on warm desk lamps and play upbeat instrumental music just to keep my spirits steady.

questions.text: Do you check the weather forecast regularly?

areSample.answer: I glance at a weather widget almost every morning before getting dressed, particularly during the rainy months.
areSample.reason: Tropical showers here can roll in out of nowhere within twenty minutes, so knowing the afternoon radar saves a thorough soaking.
areSample.example: Even so, forecasts aren't foolproof, which is why I still tuck a lightweight raincoat under my motorbike seat all year round.

questions.text: What activities do people in your area usually do when the weather is bad?

areSample.answer: When heavy rain hits, most locals either retreat to cosy cafés or gather around a steaming pot of hotpot at home.
areSample.reason: Sharing warm, comforting food turns a gloomy downpour into a rather pleasant excuse to slow down and catch up.
areSample.example: Just last Friday a sudden storm cancelled our outdoor badminton game, so six of us ended up playing board games at a friend's flat instead.

questions.text: What kind of music do you usually listen to?

areSample.answer: My taste is fairly eclectic, though I gravitate towards mellow indie folk and instrumental jazz most days.
areSample.reason: Lyrics tend to distract me when I'm reading or coding, so acoustic tracks create a steady rhythm without competing for my attention.
areSample.example: On my evening commute, however, I'll happily switch to upbeat soul or classic rock to shake off tiredness.

questions.text: Have your musical tastes changed much since you were a teenager?

areSample.answer: Quite dramatically, actually—as a teenager I listened almost exclusively to chart pop and high-energy rock.
areSample.reason: As I've got older, I've started paying much closer attention to songwriting craft, subtle harmonies, and live instrumentation.
areSample.example: I recently went back to some acoustic folk albums my father used to play in the car, and they resonate with me in a way they never did at sixteen.

questions.text: Have you ever learnt to play a musical instrument?

areSample.answer: I taught myself the basics of acoustic guitar at university, though I'd still call myself an enthusiastic amateur at best.
areSample.reason: Learning chords forced me to slow down and be patient with clumsy fingers, which was a refreshing contrast to screen-based work.
areSample.example: I don't practise as consistently as I ought to, yet strumming a couple of familiar songs on Sunday afternoons always helps me unwind.

questions.text: Do you prefer listening to recorded music or going to live concerts?

areSample.answer: Nothing quite beats the electricity of a small live venue, even though recorded music is obviously what fills my everyday life.
areSample.reason: Hearing musicians improvise on stage and sharing that atmosphere with a crowd turns a familiar track into a one-off memory.
areSample.example: A few months ago I attended an acoustic jazz trio in a tiny basement club, and the raw acoustics gave me goosebumps.

questions.text: Do you do any regular sport or physical exercise?

areSample.answer: Yes, I try to jog three mornings a week and play an hour of badminton with colleagues on Thursday evenings.
areSample.reason: Since my job keeps me hunched over a keyboard all day, moving properly is essential for both my posture and my sleep quality.
areSample.example: Even a brisk five-kilometre loop around the park clears away mental cobwebs far more effectively than a second cup of coffee.

questions.text: Do you prefer watching sports or playing them yourself?

areSample.answer: I'm much more inclined to play than to spectate, except during major international tournaments like the World Cup.
areSample.reason: Being on the court gives you an immediate adrenaline rush and a great workout, whereas sitting through a two-hour broadcast rarely holds my attention.
areSample.example: That said, I'll gladly join friends to cheer on our national football team whenever there's a big knockout match.

questions.text: Which sports are most popular in your country?

areSample.answer: Football is easily the undisputed favourite across all age groups, closely followed by badminton for everyday recreation.
areSample.reason: Both require minimal gear and can be set up almost anywhere, from school yards to quiet neighbourhood alleys.
areSample.example: If you walk through any city park at six in the morning, you'll hear the steady pop of shuttlecocks alongside groups doing brisk walking.

questions.text: Is there a sport you have never tried but would like to learn?

areSample.answer: I've been eager to try indoor bouldering for quite a while now.
areSample.reason: It appeals to me because it combines upper-body strength with physical puzzle-solving, so your mind stays completely absorbed.
areSample.example: A new climbing gym opened twenty minutes from my flat recently, and I'm planning to sign up for an introductory session next month.

questions.text: Do you like taking photographs?

areSample.answer: I do enjoy snapping candid scenes when I'm out walking or travelling, though I'm careful not to view the whole trip through a lens.
areSample.reason: Looking for good light and framing trains you to notice small architectural details you'd normally rush straight past.
areSample.example: Last weekend I caught the late-afternoon sun slanting across an old flower market, and it turned into one of my favourite shots of the year.

questions.text: Do you usually take photos with your phone or with a dedicated camera?

areSample.answer: For everyday moments I almost always use my smartphone, simply because it's already in my pocket.
areSample.reason: Phone cameras have come on in leaps and bounds, especially in low light, so lugging a bulky camera body feels unnecessary for casual outings.
areSample.example: I only borrow my brother's mirrorless camera when I'm heading into the mountains and want crisp landscape prints.

questions.text: What do you usually do with the photographs you take?

areSample.answer: Most of them sit in organised cloud albums, though I've started printing a handful of favourites at the end of each year.
areSample.reason: When thousands of images pile up on a hard drive, you hardly ever revisit them, whereas a physical print on a shelf actually sparks memories.
areSample.example: Last December I put together a slim photo book of our family trip to the highlands, and my parents still flick through it regularly.

questions.text: Do you prefer taking photos of people or of places?

areSample.answer: I lean towards places and quiet streetscapes, though an unposed shot of friends laughing is always priceless.
areSample.reason: Staged portraits tend to look stiff and awkward, whereas landscapes or candid moments capture the genuine mood of a setting.
areSample.example: My favourite photo from a recent hike isn't the group selfie at the summit, but a shot of mist drifting over a quiet valley below.

questions.text: Do you enjoy travelling to new places?

areSample.answer: Yes, travelling is easily the thing I look forward to most each year, provided I don't cram too many stops into one itinerary.
areSample.reason: Stepping out of familiar surroundings shakes up your routine and gives you fresh perspective on everyday problems back home.
areSample.example: Even a quiet four-day break in a hill town leaves me feeling far more restored than a week spent resting indoors.

questions.text: Do you prefer travelling alone or with other people?

areSample.answer: My sweet spot is travelling with one or two close friends whose pace matches mine, though I've also enjoyed the odd solo trip.
areSample.reason: Sharing a stunning view or an unexpected mishap with someone makes the memory twice as rich, without the compromises of a huge tour group.
areSample.example: When I visited Kyoto with a friend last year, we agreed to split up for a couple of afternoons so we could each explore our own interests.

questions.text: How do you usually plan a holiday before you go?

areSample.answer: I like to pin down the essentials—flights, accommodation, and one or two must-see sights—while leaving the rest delightfully loose.
areSample.reason: Over-scheduling every hour turns a holiday into a logistical checklist and leaves no room for local recommendations.
areSample.example: Some of my best meals abroad happened simply because a café owner scribbled the name of a tucked-away noodle shop on a napkin.

questions.text: Is there a place you have visited that you would love to return to?

areSample.answer: I'd jump at the chance to revisit Da Lat in the central highlands, ideally for a full week rather than a flying weekend.
areSample.reason: The cool pine-scented air and slower rhythm feel worlds away from coastal humidity, and I barely scratched the surface of its hiking trails.
areSample.example: Next time I'd love to rent a quiet cabin on the outskirts and spend mornings writing with a view of the valley fog.

questions.text: Which social media platforms do you use most often?

areSample.answer: I mainly use messaging apps to stay in touch with family, along with YouTube and a couple of niche discussion forums.
areSample.reason: Long-form channels actually teach me something useful, whereas endless short-video feeds tend to swallow half an hour before I realise it.
areSample.example: Over the past year I've followed several architecture and linguistics creators whose breakdowns I watch while folding laundry.

questions.text: How much time do you think you spend on social media each day?

areSample.answer: I try to keep it under forty-five minutes a day, though it occasionally creeps past an hour when I'm tired after work.
areSample.reason: Because algorithms are engineered to hold your eye, it's remarkably easy to lose track of time unless you put friction in place.
areSample.example: Setting a built-in app timer on my phone that dims the screen after thirty minutes has cut my mindless scrolling dramatically.

questions.text: Do you prefer posting your own updates or mostly reading what others share?

areSample.answer: I'm very much a quiet observer—I probably post a public update only two or three times a year.
areSample.reason: I'm quite protective of my privacy, and I'd rather send a quick photo directly to a group chat of close friends than broadcast it to acquaintances.
areSample.example: When I finished a half-marathon recently, I just texted a picture to my family and three running buddies instead of putting it on a public feed.

questions.text: Do you think people rely too heavily on social media for news nowadays?

areSample.answer: Yes, to a worrying degree, because viral headlines often reward outrage rather than accuracy or nuance.
areSample.reason: A complex economic or scientific story simply can't be understood from a thirty-second clip stripped of context.
areSample.example: Whenever I see a dramatic claim trending on a feed, I make a point of checking two established news outlets before taking it seriously.
